It is just an old, ingrained trope. Something similar is from older cinema in a certain East Asian country, where when a character would be introduced, the screen would freeze and their name would appear. I don't think it's a matter of telling and not showing, especially given how your example includes them showing. It exists in fighting games too. When a specific character does a specific special move, you know it's that move, you don't have to take his word for it. It's not meant to handhold the viewer and explain what it is, I think it's just a dramatic element of introduction that western audiences may differ on.

> Your example of fighting games is actually a very prime example, they are special attack/techniques that the characters often name out so that you, the player(s) are aware they are special and different, and not just a simple combo move.

Then why isn't it done for every special move? Character A and Character B rarely do it, for example. Character C cries out the name of his fireball or dragon punch, but there are on screen visual indicators that these aren't just punches, they're flaming, they look special. Meanwhile Character A's specials are still just punches, and they don't have any accompanying name telegraphing. Surely if the naming of moves had to do with balance and hand holding, everyone one do it to make a fair, especially the guy whose normals and specials are both punches with decidedly less fire radiating off of them.

Instead the ones getting audibly introduced are the ones that also have visual recognition - the recognizable special moves that a seasoned player could identify long before the character starts talking about it - because the introduction is for drama, not gameplay.

Anyone playing can tell that a hadoken, even before a certain character yells, is not just a normal punch. The naming has nothing to do with it, he's throwing a fucking fireball. But at the same time, a certain other character is never shouting out the names of his moves, which normal or input, are still just mundane punches.

Yes, the shout does help player response in a way, but I highly doubt that was intentional, it just become a way to time the move because it was happening. 

The moves that get audible names are often the most flashy of the special moves, which leads me to think it is entirely similar to how it's used in movies/shows.

>but instead created a precedent for other games to learn from. Powerful moves in most modern games have some sort of flashy way to signify what is happening and the easiest way to do that is to have a character tell you.

As someone else said, even more fighting games *don't* do this. 

>It also makes games more accessible because even a new player understands that the enemy isn't going to shout out weak and ordinary move names so they know to block

Many characters, even in SF, don't do it. None of Balrog's special punches have a visual or audible key to set them apart from normal punches. 

I agree that the naming of the move does help to some degree, but it's an unintended side effect.

>however the first anime series that did it, their reasoning was as I said

[citation needed]

That said, I think we're just saying the same thing in different ways. I don't see it has handholding, I see it as a different culture's way of heightening the drama for a specific situation. It's a very eastern cliche that is rooted in traditions that don't really exist on the other side of the world. You don't need to hear a narrative explanation to know why the protagonist's fireball beam thing is any stronger than his punch, or even any other fireball - there's all kind of pageantry around it that does it other than simply giving it a name. Giving it the name isn't skipping the story telling to tell you that it's now suddenly stronger, giving the name/sounds to go with it [*makes it stronger*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiai). Eastern cinema, and a lot of the culture, just really likes verbosity and titling things that don't really need an introduction - which what the OP is referencing in the first places. 

The audience will realize it's stronger without the quirk. Most anime, especially older ones, use a lot of recycled footage of long start ups and "powering up" for strong moves. It has nothing to do with shouting its name - even if that may often be a part of it.
